questions.prompt: A continuous real-valued function on a nonempty compact subset of real space
options: attains its minimum and its maximum
attains its minimum only when the set is a ball
can be unbounded on that set
questions.explanation: This is the extreme-value conclusion in real space: continuity plus a nonempty compact domain gives an attained minimum and an attained maximum. The function need not be constant. Compactness is closed and bounded, not a requirement that the set be a ball. A continuous function on a compact set is bounded.

questions.prompt: Minimize \((x - 3)^2 + y^2\) over the closed unit disk \(x^2 + y^2 \le 1\). What is the minimum value?
questions.explanation: The unconstrained bowl opens at \((3, 0)\), which lies outside the disk. On the disk the expression is the squared distance to \((3, 0)\), so the minimum is the squared distance from \((3, 0)\) to the nearest feasible point. That point is \((1, 0)\), and the squared distance is \(4\). Reporting 9 uses the squared distance from the origin to \((3, 0)\) and ignores the disk. Reporting 1 gives a coordinate of the contact point. The value 0 is the unconstrained minimum and is not feasible.

questions.prompt: A function \(f\) on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is coercive when
options: \(f(x)\) tends to \(+\infty\) as \(\lVert x \rVert\) tends to infinity
every sublevel set of \(f\) is open
questions.explanation: Coercivity is a statement about the behavior at infinity: the function eventually exceeds every height. A bounded function fails it. A stationary point is a derivative fact and can exist without coercivity, as with a sine. Sublevel sets of a continuous function are closed, not open, and coercivity is what makes the low ones bounded.
questions.figure_alt: A curve of one variable, drawn on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: Put these checks in the order used to argue that a minimizer exists.
questions.explanation: Emptiness ends the argument at once. A nonempty compact set is the direct extreme-value case, and it does not need a coercivity test. On an unbounded set the compact-set theorem does not apply, so the next check is whether sublevel sets are bounded, which is what coercivity gives. Only after that check does the unbounded case conclude. Testing coercivity on a set that is already compact is unnecessary, and it is the wrong tool for an empty set.

steps: If the feasible set is empty, stop: no minimizer exists.
If the feasible set is nonempty and compact and the objective is continuous, conclude that a minimizer exists.
If the feasible set is unbounded, test whether the objective tends to infinity as the norm does.
If that coercivity test passes and the objective is continuous, conclude that a minimizer exists.

questions.prompt: Which of these functions attain a global minimum on the stated domain?
questions.explanation:
The square \(t^2\) is continuous and coercive, so it attains the value 0. On the compact interval \([0, 3]\) the identity attains 0 at the endpoint. The sine attains \(-1\).
• The exponential gets arbitrarily close to 0 and never reaches it.
• On the open interval the values get arbitrarily close to 0 and every positive value is still beaten by a smaller feasible input, so the infimum is not attained.
The sine shows that coercivity is sufficient, not necessary: it attains its minimum without tending to infinity.
questions.figure_alt: A curve of one variable, drawn on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: Minimize \(t + 1/t\) over \(t > 0\). What is the minimum value?
questions.explanation: The derivative is \(1 - 1/t^2\), which vanishes at \(t = 1\) on the positive line. The second derivative \(2/t^3\) is positive there, so the critical point is a local minimizer, and the value is \(1 + 1 = 2\). The same conclusion follows from \((\sqrt{t} - 1/\sqrt{t})^2 \ge 0\), which rearranges to \(t + 1/t \ge 2\). As \(t\) approaches 0 or infinity the function tends to infinity, so the local minimizer is global. Reporting 1 gives the location. Reporting 0 is not a value of this function.
questions.figure_alt: A curve of one variable, drawn on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: A note claims that \(e^{-t}\) attains its minimum on the half-line \(t \ge 0\). Exactly one step is false.
questions.explanation: The exponential is continuous, the extreme-value statement is right, and closed bounded subsets of the line are compact. The false step is the claim that the half-line is bounded. It is closed and unbounded, so the compact-set theorem does not apply. The function decreases toward 0 and never reaches it, so the infimum is not attained.
questions.figure_alt: A curve of one variable, drawn on labeled axes.
steps: The half-line \(t \ge 0\) is closed and bounded.
A continuous function attains its minimum on a nonempty compact set.
A closed and bounded subset of the real line is compact.
reasons: The half-line is closed and unbounded, so it is not compact.
A continuous function on a nonempty compact set need not attain its minimum.

questions.prompt: A continuous coercive function on a nonempty closed set
options: attains a minimum only if that set is bounded
questions.explanation: Coercivity makes every sublevel set bounded. Continuity makes it closed. A nonempty closed set supplies at least one feasible value, so some sublevel set is nonempty, hence compact, and the function attains its minimum there. The set itself may be unbounded. The function need not be constant. The sublevel set at a feasible height is nonempty.
questions.figure_alt: A curve of one variable, drawn on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: Let \(f(x, y) = x^2 + 4y^2 + 6\) on the plane. What is the global minimum value?
questions.explanation: Both squares are nonnegative, so \(f \ge 6\), and equality holds at the origin. The function is a polynomial, hence continuous, and it tends to infinity as the norm does, so the lower bound is attained. Reporting 4 uses the coefficient of \(y^2\). Reporting 1 would be the value of a square that this function does not have at the origin. Reporting 10 is \(f(2, 0)\), which is larger.

questions.prompt: Existence of a minimizer does not name the point. For a smooth coercive function the minimizer is among
options: the points where the function is negative
the boundary of the unit ball, always
the eigenvectors of the Hessian only
questions.explanation: A coercive smooth function attains a minimum, and an interior minimizer on an open domain has gradient zero. Finding the stationary points is the next search. The minimum value need not be negative. The unit ball is one compact set, not the location of every minimizer. Eigenvectors describe the Hessian, not the list of candidate points.

questions.prompt: Let \(f(t) = t^4 - 4t\) on the real line. What is the global minimum value?
questions.explanation: The derivative is \(4t^3 - 4 = 4(t^3 - 1)\), so the only real stationary point is \(t = 1\). The value there is \(1 - 4 = -3\). The second derivative \(12t^2\) is positive at \(t = 1\), and \(t^4\) dominates as \(\lvert t \rvert\) grows, so the function is coercive and this stationary value is the global minimum. Reporting 1 gives the location. Reporting \(-4\) drops the fourth-power term. Reporting 4 is the derivative coefficient, not a function value at the minimizer.
questions.figure_alt: A curve of one variable, drawn on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: Minimize \(e^{x}\) over the plane. This problem
options: has every point as a minimizer
has optimal value 1, attained at the origin
has a minimizer at the origin because the gradient vanishes there
questions.explanation: For every point, moving left in \(x\) multiplies the value by a number smaller than 1, so no point is a local minimizer and none is global. The infimum is 0 and it is not attained. The origin has value 1 and gradient \((1, 0)\), which is not zero. The exponential is positive, so 1 is not a lower bound.
questions.figure_alt: A curve of one variable, drawn on labeled axes.
